answer: SkipGram does not explicitly use a Wikipedia word graph or network at all. It is a shallow neural language model (Mikolov et al., 2013) that learns dense word vectors by training on raw word co-occurrence within local context windows: for each target word it is trained to predict surrounding context words, using negative sampling or hierarchical softmax. Its word-analogy performance (e.g., king - man + woman ≈ queen) emerges from the geometry of these learned embeddings, which capture regularities in the distributional statistics of the text corpus, not from traversing or propagating over a pre-built graph. Graph-based methods, by contrast, explicitly construct a network of words (nodes linked by co-occurrence or semantic relations, such as Wikipedia link or category graphs) and derive representations from its structure, for example via random walks (DeepWalk, node2vec), spreading activation, or graph propagation. So the premise that SkipGram uses the Wikipedia word network is mistaken; the contrast is that SkipGram learns from sequential text windows, whereas graph methods learn from an explicit graph structure. (If a specific paper compared SkipGram against a graph-based method on Wikipedia, its details would be needed to answer more precisely.)
